reason: The sources provide strong multi-source corroboration across independent domains for discovery, measurements, naming history, and cosmological controversies.
story: In 2013, astronomers mapping cosmic explosions uncovered a structure so colossal it broke the standard rules of astrophysics. Led by Istvan Horvath, Jon Hakkila, and Zsolt Bagoly, the team analyzed gamma-ray bursts recorded by NASA's Swift satellite and discovered an unprecedented concentration of bursts near the constellations Hercules and Corona Borealis. Because gamma-ray bursts trace the deaths of massive stars in distant galaxies, this clustering revealed an enormous galactic superstructure spanning roughly 10 billion light-years—more than ten percent of the entire observable universe. Dubbed the Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall by a Filipino teenager on Wikipedia, the behemoth directly defies the cosmological principle, which holds that matter should be evenly distributed on scales larger than 1.2 billion light-years. While critics argue the wall might be a statistical illusion born from uneven sky surveys, scientists await future missions like the THESEUS space telescope to confirm whether this cosmic titan truly exists.
angle: Astronomers detected a cosmic superstructure spanning 10 billion light-years—a tenth of the observable universe—that is theoretically too massive to exist under our standard laws of cosmology.

claims.claim: The Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall was discovered in 2013 by an astronomical team led by Istvan Horvath, Jon Hakkila, and Zsolt Bagoly.
The structure was detected through statistical mapping of gamma-ray burst locations across the sky.
Data for identifying the burst clustering came from NASA's Swift space telescope alongside ground-based observatories.
Gamma-ray bursts serve as indirect beacons to map massive cosmic structures because they originate from massive stars and extreme stellar events like supernovae and neutron star collisions.
The structure was originally calculated to span approximately 10 billion light-years across.
At 10 billion light-years in length, the structure spans roughly 10 to 11 percent of the observable universe's diameter.
The clustering is located in the direction of the constellations Hercules and Corona Borealis.
The original cluster detection was centered at a redshift range between 1.6 and 2.1.
The name 'Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall' was coined by a Filipino teenager on Wikipedia rather than the discovering astronomers.
The name is considered a misnomer because the structure extends into other constellations such as Bootes and Draco, and appears roundish rather than wall-like.
In the initial discovery dataset, 14 out of 31 gamma-ray bursts in that specific redshift shell clustered in one sky region.
The structure challenges the cosmological principle, which posits the universe is homogeneous and should not contain structures larger than approximately 1.2 billion light-years.
In 2020, astronomer Sam Christian published research arguing the perceived clustering could be an artifact of statistical or experimental bias.
Astronomers have stated that a future dedicated space telescope mission, ESA's THESEUS, will be required to conclusively confirm or disprove the wall's existence.
Subsequent research analyzing 542 gamma-ray bursts suggested the structure may extend up to 15 billion light-years across.

disputed: Whether the structure is a genuine physical galaxy superstructure or a statistical artifact caused by uneven satellite sky coverage and observational biases (attribute: critics like Sam Christian treat it as doubtful, while the discoverers maintain the signal is real in updated datasets).

The true physical length and redshift extent of the structure, ranging from the original 10 billion light-years at redshift 1.6 to 2.1 to later estimates of 15 billion light-years spanning redshift 0.33 to 2.43 (attribute: according to follow-up studies).
